title: Computer Organisation
description: Performance, number representation, caches, pipelines, virtual memory, I/O and storage. Every calculation is computed, not estimated.

platforms.name: Nand2Tetris
platforms.note: Build a computer from logic gates, free course

questions.title: CPU performance equation
questions.prompt: A program executes 3 × 10⁹ instructions with an average CPI of 1.4 on a 2.8 GHz CPU. How long does it take? What are the three ways to make it faster?
questions.answer:
CPU time = IC × CPI / clock rate = (3 × 10⁹ × 1.4) / (2.8 × 10⁹) = **1.5 s**.

The three factors are instruction count (better algorithm, compiler or ISA), CPI (better microarchitecture: pipelining, caches, branch prediction) and clock rate (technology, limited by power). Comparing machines by clock rate or MIPS alone is misleading, because a different ISA does a different amount of work per instruction: compare execution time of the same program.

questions.title: Amdahl's law
questions.prompt: 70% of a program's run time is made 5 times faster. What is the overall speedup, and what is the best possible speedup however much that part is accelerated?
questions.answer: Speedup = 1 / ((1 − 0.7) + 0.7/5) = 1 / (0.3 + 0.14) = **2.27**. The limit is 1 / (1 − 0.7) = **3.33**, set by the 30% that is untouched. Lesson: optimise the common case, but the part you do not speed up eventually dominates; this is also why adding cores helps programs with large serial sections so little.

questions.title: Two's complement
questions.prompt: Write −45 as an 8-bit two's complement number. What is the range of 8-bit two's complement, and why does the same adder work for signed and unsigned numbers?
questions.answer:
+45 = 00101101. Invert all bits: 11010010. Add 1: **11010011**. Check: −128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = −45.

The 8-bit range is **−128 to +127**. The same adder works because in two's complement the sign bit simply has weight −2ⁿ⁻¹ and arithmetic is done modulo 2ⁿ: adding the bit patterns gives the right pattern for both interpretations, only the interpretation of overflow differs (carry out for unsigned, sign change for signed).

questions.title: Encoding a floating-point number
questions.prompt: Encode −6.25 as an IEEE 754 single-precision number and give the hexadecimal pattern.
questions.answer:
6.25 = 110.01₂ = 1.1001 × 2². Sign = 1 (negative). Exponent = 2 + 127 = 129 = **10000001**. Fraction = the digits after the leading 1: 1001 padded to 23 bits = **10010000000000000000000**.

Bits: 1 | 10000001 | 10010000000000000000000 = **0xC0C80000**.

Check by decoding: (−1)¹ × 1.5625 × 4 = −6.25. Remember the hidden leading 1, the bias of 127, and that the exponent field is stored unsigned.

questions.title: Cache address fields
questions.prompt: A 32-bit address is used with a 64 KB 2-way set-associative cache with 32-byte blocks. How many bits are in the tag, index and offset?
questions.answer:
Offset = log₂ 32 = **5** bits. Blocks = 64 KB / 32 B = 2048. Sets = 2048 / 2 = 1024, so index = **10** bits. Tag = 32 − 10 − 5 = **17** bits.

A direct-mapped cache of the same size would have 2048 sets (11 index bits, 16 tag bits); fully associative would have no index (27 tag bits). More associativity means a longer tag and more comparators, with fewer conflict misses.

questions.title: Average memory access time with two cache levels
questions.prompt: L1 has a 2 ns hit time and an 8% local miss rate. L2 has a 12 ns hit time and a 25% local miss rate. Main memory takes 120 ns. Find the average memory access time.
questions.answer:
AMAT = H₁ + m₁ × (H₂ + m₂ × T_mem) = 2 + 0.08 × (12 + 0.25 × 120) = 2 + 0.08 × 42 = **5.36 ns**.

The L1 miss penalty is itself an average: the L2 hit time plus L2's misses going to memory. Use **local** miss rates (misses divided by accesses to that level); the global L2 miss rate is 0.08 × 0.25 = 2%.

questions.title: Pipeline speedup with stalls
questions.prompt: A 5-stage pipeline runs 500 instructions and loses 40 cycles to stalls. How many cycles does it take and what is the speedup over a non-pipelined machine that takes 5 cycles per instruction?
questions.answer:
Cycles = k + n − 1 + stalls = 5 + 500 − 1 + 40 = **544**. The non-pipelined machine needs 500 × 5 = 2,500 cycles, so speedup = 2500 / 544 ≈ **4.60**.

Without the stalls it would be 2500 / 504 ≈ 4.96, close to the ideal 5. Stalls come from data hazards (load-use), control hazards (branches) and structural hazards; forwarding, branch prediction and instruction scheduling reduce them.

questions.title: Pipeline hazards
questions.prompt: Name the three types of pipeline hazard and one remedy for each. Why does a load-use dependence still need a stall with forwarding?
questions.answer:
**Structural:** two instructions need the same hardware (one memory port for fetch and data): separate instruction and data caches. **Data:** an instruction needs a result not produced yet (RAW): forwarding/bypassing, or compiler scheduling. **Control:** a branch changes the PC and the next instructions were fetched too early: branch prediction, delayed branches, or stalling.

A load's data is available only at the end of the MEM stage, after the following instruction's EX stage has started, so even with forwarding an immediately dependent instruction must wait **one** cycle (the load-use stall). The compiler can fill that slot with an independent instruction.

questions.title: Effective access time with a TLB
questions.prompt: The TLB hit ratio is 95%, a TLB lookup takes 4 ns and a memory access takes 60 ns. With a single-level page table, what is the effective memory access time?
questions.answer:
Hit: 4 + 60 = 64 ns. Miss: 4 + 60 (page table) + 60 (data) = 124 ns. EAT = 0.95 × 64 + 0.05 × 124 = **67 ns**.

Without a TLB every access would cost 120 ns, so the TLB nearly halves it. Multi-level page tables make a miss costlier (one extra access per level), so a high TLB hit ratio matters even more; locality is what delivers it.

questions.title: Hamming code
questions.prompt: How many check bits does a single-error-correcting Hamming code need for 32 data bits? How does SECDED differ?
questions.answer:
We need 2ʳ ≥ m + r + 1 = 32 + r + 1. For r = 5: 32 ≥ 38 is false; for r = **6**: 64 ≥ 39 is true. So 6 check bits (a 38-bit codeword). The check bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32; the **syndrome** (which parity checks fail) gives the position of the flipped bit.

**SECDED** adds one overall parity bit (7 here): it corrects any single-bit error and **detects** (but cannot correct) double-bit errors. ECC server memory uses SECDED on 64 data bits with 8 check bits.

questions.title: Endianness
questions.prompt: How is the 32-bit value 0x12345678 stored at address 1000 on a little-endian and on a big-endian machine?
questions.answer: **Little-endian** (x86, most ARM systems) stores the least significant byte first: addresses 1000 to 1003 hold **78 56 34 12**. **Big-endian** (network byte order) stores the most significant byte first: 12 34 56 78. It matters when reading binary files, sending data over sockets between different machines, or inspecting memory. Java's `ByteBuffer` defaults to big-endian; use `order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN)` to change it.

questions.title: Disk access time
questions.prompt: A 10,000 rpm disk has a 3 ms average seek, 512-byte sectors and 400 sectors per track. How long does it take to read an 8 KB block on one track?
questions.answer:
Rotation takes 60,000 / 10,000 = 6 ms, so the average rotational latency is 3 ms. The track holds 512 × 400 = 204,800 bytes, so transferring 8,192 bytes takes 8192 / 204800 × 6 ≈ 0.24 ms. Total = 3 + 3 + 0.24 ≈ **6.24 ms**.

Seek and rotation dominate, which is why random disk I/O is slow and why databases and file systems favour sequential access, big blocks and caching. An SSD has no seek or rotation.

questions.title: RAID levels
questions.prompt: Six 8 TB disks are used in RAID 5. What is the usable capacity, and how many failures can it survive? Compare RAID 0, 1, 5 and 10.
questions.answer: RAID 5 usable capacity = (N − 1) × C = 5 × 8 = **40 TB**; it survives **one** disk failure (a lost block is the XOR of the other blocks of its stripe). RAID 0 stripes with no redundancy (N × C, no failures survived, fastest). RAID 1 mirrors (N × C / 2, survives one failure per pair). RAID 10 is a stripe of mirrors (N × C / 2, good for databases). RAID 5 has a small-write penalty (read old data and parity, write new data and parity) and a risky rebuild on very large disks, which is why RAID 6 (two parity blocks) is often preferred.

questions.title: RISC versus CISC
questions.prompt: Compare RISC and CISC. Is x86 CISC or RISC today?
questions.answer: **RISC** (ARM, RISC-V, MIPS): a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions, a **load/store architecture** (only loads and stores touch memory), many registers, easy pipelining, typically hardwired control. **CISC** (x86): many complex variable-length instructions, memory operands, fewer registers, often microprogrammed control, smaller code. The x86 **instruction set** is CISC, but modern cores **decode each instruction into RISC-like micro-operations** and execute those in a deeply pipelined, out-of-order core, so the difference now lives mainly in the ISA and decode cost: ARM's simple decoding is one reason it is power-efficient.
